Welcome Boo. Thank you Mary. Good evening Mayor and Council. It is with great pride and excitement that I share with you a remarkable
achievement for the City's sanitary and stormwater utilities and parks and
cemeteries divisions. This is an achievement that reflects our joint
commitment to environmental stewardship, climate resilience and community well-being. Last week,
the Montgomery Creek Rehabilitation Project received the Ontario Public Works Association's
2024 Project of the Year Award in the Environmental Climate Resilient Infrastructure category.
This prestigious recognition celebrates innovation, sustainability and excellence in public
infrastructure. The project rehabilitated a 500-meter section of Montgomery Creek
originally channelized in the 1960s to manage storm water. While effective at the time, this
approach often shifted flooding and pollution downstream. With climate change increasing the
intensity of storms, these flooding and pollution impacts would have become more severe for the
Montgomery Creek. Additionally, the creek was never designed to enhance biodiversity
or achieve other co-benefits for the area. We knew we could do better and we did.
We implemented a nature-based solution that not only addressed stormwater challenges,
but also created a vibrant community-focused green space.
Key features included natural meanders, wetlands, and native vegetation to manage stormwater and reduce flood risk,
a widened creek channel that absorbs and slows stormwater, protecting infrastructure and ecosystems.
While 70 mature trees were removed to expand the creek, we planted over 700 trees and 4,000
native shrubs, enhancing habitat, cooling the area, and supporting pollinators and other
wildlife. Through engagement with Indigenous rights holders, we included culturally significant
plantings to support traditional foraging. The rehabilitated creek has also enhanced
fish habitat that now supports species like black-nosed dace and creek chub.
Community engagement also led to creative reuse of felled trees for habitat, play and
education, honouring both the ecological and cultural values of the community.
A new full-span bridge and trail upgrades restored safe year-round access between neighbourhoods
and amenities.
Thoughtfully designed creek elements now invite residents to safely engage with the water,
deepening the connection to nature.
To celebrate the project's completion, we hosted an opening and planting event with
the community.
This was an opportunity to further engage residents, showcase the space's unique features,
and invite community members to contribute to the new community space.
What began as a stormwater management challenge has become a shining example of how nature-based
solutions can transform not only our landscapes, but also the way we live, connect and thrive
as a community.
Before I conclude, I wanted to recognize the contributions of the City of Kitchener's
sanitary and stormwater utilities and Parks and Cemetery's project teams, whose tireless
